endorsements.quote: PF-AI should always be paired with an equivalent staff-assisted fallback, such as interpreter-supported intake, bedside staff engagement, or standard nondigital workflows, so patients who cannot or do not wish to engage digitally are not excluded.
The safest model is human-in-the-loop: generative AI drafts patient instructions, and clinicians review, edit, and contextualize content before release.
A practical safety boundary is that PF-AI should not independently determine emergency triage level, final diagnosis, definitive treatment plans, or discharge of potentially unstable patients.

Institutions should predefine accountability matrices spanning vendors, health systems, supervising clinicians, and operational review teams, with auditable logs for every high-risk recommendation and override decision.

As part of a learning health system, programs should monitor process and outcome metrics: engagement, recommendation accuracy, override rates, clinician time burden, left-without-being-seen, return visits, follow-up completion, patient complaints, adverse events, and subgroup performance by language, literacy, race/ethnicity, insurance status, age, and digital access.

Because emergency physicians cannot reasonably review all generated content, oversight should be role-stratified: frontline nurses or quality coordinators review low-risk outputs, physicians adjudicate high-risk or discordant recommendations, and medical directors oversee periodic quality audits and model updates.
The key question is not whether artificial intelligence is available, but whether it adds measurable value over existing workflows for specific ED populations and tasks.

unlisted_practices: Use clear disclosure and nonanthropomorphic design cues so patients know they are interacting with an automated system rather than a clinician.
Map every outbound AI check-in to a defined backend action owner with response-time targets.
Implement data protection lifecycle governance including explicit consent language, granular access controls, defined retention limits, and patient controls to disconnect data sources.
Verify platform Business Associate Agreement coverage and consult privacy officers before entering protected health information into public generative AI tools.
Establish community-based participatory codesign with compensated community partners who hold authority to trigger mitigation, pause, or sunset of a deployed tool.
Use numerical denominators, absolute risk differences, and icon arrays rather than vague verbal probability terms when communicating risk to patients.
Do not let AI delay safety-critical nursing triage or emergency stabilization; collect supplemental information only after minimum triage safeguards.
Trigger immediate nurse reassessment for any high-risk symptom change rather than automated reassurance, and label wait-time estimates as dynamic projections.
Track whether digital diversion to virtual pathways shifts burden onto patients with fewer resources.
